reference.source: ESC/AHA cardiomyopathy and pericardial/myocardial disease guidelines; Braunwald's Heart Disease
clinicalPearls: A form of eosinophilic endomyocardial disease occurring in the setting of persistent hypereosinophilia, leading to a restrictive cardiomyopathy
Despite the name, it is a non-infective inflammatory and fibrotic process rather than infective endocarditis
Cardiac involvement evolves through an acute necrotic phase, a thrombotic phase and a late fibrotic phase with endomyocardial scarring
Mural thrombus within the ventricular apices and along the inflow tract predisposes to systemic embolism
Fibrosis and thrombus can tether the atrioventricular valves and obliterate the ventricular cavities, producing restrictive physiology and valvular regurgitation
Underlying causes of the eosinophilia include primary (clonal) and secondary hypereosinophilic syndromes, and it overlaps with tropical endomyocardial fibrosis

Treatment targets the eosinophilia (for example corticosteroids and cause-specific therapy) alongside heart failure management, anticoagulation for thrombus and surgery for advanced valvular or fibrotic disease
Cardiac MRI is valuable for detecting thrombus, inflammation and the characteristic endomyocardial fibrosis
reference.pathophysiology: Loeffler endocarditis results from sustained hypereosinophilia in which activated eosinophils infiltrate the endomyocardium and release toxic granule proteins. These damage the endocardium and myocardium, initiating an acute necrotic and inflammatory phase. Endocardial injury then promotes mural thrombus formation, and over time organising thrombus and reactive fibrosis produce dense endomyocardial scarring. The resulting stiff, non-compliant ventricles impair filling to cause restrictive cardiomyopathy, while fibrosis and thrombus involving the subvalvular apparatus lead to atrioventricular valve regurgitation and apical cavity obliteration. Systemic embolism from mural thrombus is an important complication.
additionalDifferentials: Other restrictive cardiomyopathies such as cardiac amyloidosis
Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis with cardiac involvement
Infective endocarditis with intracardiac thrombus or vegetation
Cardiac tumour or apical thrombus of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film confirming and quantifying eosinophilia
Echocardiography for apical thrombus, endomyocardial thickening, valve involvement and restrictive filling
Cardiac MRI for thrombus, inflammation and endomyocardial fibrosis
Investigation of the cause of eosinophilia (clonal markers, secondary causes, parasitic and allergic screens)
Cardiac biomarkers and assessment of embolic complications
redFlags: Signs of heart failure with restrictive physiology in a patient with marked eosinophilia
Systemic embolic event from intracardiac thrombus
Rapidly progressive valvular regurgitation or cavity obliteration
Very high or rising eosinophil count with cardiac symptoms
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on early control of the eosinophilia and the extent of endomyocardial fibrosis; treatment during the earlier phases can limit damage, whereas established fibrotic restrictive disease carries a poor prognosis with heart failure and embolic risk.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for infective endocarditis because of the name
Overlooking mild eosinophilia and failing to link it to the cardiac picture
Missing apical mural thrombus and the consequent need for anticoagulation
Delaying treatment of the eosinophilia until irreversible fibrosis has developed
Not investigating the underlying cause of the hypereosinophilia
references: ESC Guidelines for the management of cardiomyopathies
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Start corticosteroids as first-line therapy to suppress the hypereosinophilia and limit endomyocardial damage
Treat the underlying cause of eosinophilia, using imatinib for FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive clonal disease, other cytoreduction such as hydroxycarbamide, and treatment of secondary or parasitic causes
Anticoagulate for mural thrombus to prevent systemic embolism
Give heart failure therapy for the restrictive physiology, including diuretics and standard measures
Undertake surgery in the fibrotic phase, including endocardial decortication and atrioventricular valve repair or replacement
Monitor disease phase and response with serial echocardiography, cardiac MRI and eosinophil counts
Manage jointly across cardiology and haematology
